'''''Physocarpus opulifolius''''',  [[common name|known as]] '''common ninebark''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''Eastern ninebark''', '''Atlantic ninebark''', or simply '''ninebark''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the rose [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Rosaceae, [[native plant|native]] to eastern North America, named for its peeling multi-hued bark.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Good Plant Guide |publisher=[[DK Publishers]] |year=1998 |isbn=978 1 4093 4986 0 |editor-last=Sarkar |editor-first=Shashwati T |edition=1st}}</ref>

==Description==
It is a mound-shaped [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] with alternate, simple [[leaf|leaves]], on arching stems. It has a height from {{convert|3|-|10|ft|m|0|abbr=on|disp=flip}} and a spread of {{convert|4|-|6|ft|m|0|abbr=on|disp=flip}}.<ref name=Kemper>{{cite web|title=Physocarpus opulifolius|url=http://www.mobot.org/gardeninghelp/plantfinder/plant.asp?code=G840|work=Kemper Center for Home Gardening|publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden|accessdate=25 September 2011|archive-date=15 July 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170715175922/http://www.mobot.org/gardeninghelp/plantfinder/plant.asp?code=G840|url-status=dead}}</ref> The leaves vary from {{convert|3|-|12|cm|0|abbr=on}} in length, with palmately veined lobes.<ref name=Neesom>[https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_phop.pdf Guy Nesom, 2000. Atlantic ninebark: ''Physocarpus opulifolius'' (L.) Maxim., Plant Symbol = PHOP. USDA Plant Guide]</ref> It is fast-growing, insect- and disease-resistant, and drought-tolerant.<ref name=LBJ>{{cite web|title=Physocarpus opulifolius (Atlantic Ninebark)|url=http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=PHOP|publisher=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center-The University of Texas at Austin|accessdate=27 September 2011}}</ref> The species is adaptable to a very wide range of soil and site conditions, from moist to dry, acid to alkaline, and gravelly to heavy clay; and can grow in partial shade to full sun.<ref name=Hoss>{{cite journal|last=Hoss|first=Gregory|title=Propagation Protocol for Ninebark (''Physocarpus opulifolius'')|journal=Native Plants Journal|year=2001|volume=2|issue=1|pages=60–61|doi=10.3368/npj.2.1.60|doi-access=free}}</ref> The 5-petaled, {{convert|6–8|mm|abbr=on}} diameter flowers form in [[corymbs]].<ref name=Hoss/> The flowers are white to pinkish, blooming from May to June in North America.<ref name=Hoss/> In Missouri the fruits ripen from August to early October and are small, dry pods hanging in drooping, papery clusters. The bark peels off in thin papery strips, exposing brown inner bark. One explanation of the common name 'ninebark' is that the peels resemble the number nine in shape.<ref name=Hoss/>
[[File:Physocarpus opulifolius.jpg|thumb|Microscopic image of a cross-section of the stalk of ''P. opulifolius'']]

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Physocarpus opulifolius 016.jpg|thumb|left|Inflorescences, [[Deschambault-Grondines]], [[Quebec]], Canada]]
''Physocarpus opulifolius'' is found in eastern North America on rocky hillsides and banks of streams<ref name=Neesom/> as well as in moist thickets, especially in counties south of the [[Missouri River]].<ref name=Kemper/> There is also a scarcely distinguishable form in the Rocky Mountain region and the Pacific Northwest.<ref>{{cite book|last=Johnson|first=Arthur|title=Taxonomy of the Flowering Plants|url=https://archive.org/details/taxonomyofflower00john|url-access=registration|year=1931|publisher=The Century Co.|location=New York|pages=[https://archive.org/details/taxonomyofflower00john/page/297 297–298]}}</ref> Its native range is from New York to Minnesota and South Dakota, south to Florida, Arkansas and Kansas. But it can be found from Quebec west to Minnesota, South Dakota and Colorado, south to Oklahoma to Georgia and north to New York.<ref name=Hoss/> The shrub is an escape, or a wild plant formerly cultivated, northeastward.<ref name=LBJ/>

==Uses==
The ability of ''P. opulifolius'' to grow in harsh conditions makes it especially suitable for erosion control on banks.<ref name=Kemper/> But it is also grown for its ornamental foliage. Numerous [[cultivars]] have been developed, of which 'Dart's Gold',<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Physocarpus opulifolius'' 'Dart's Gold'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/96334/Physocarpus-opulifolius-Dart-s-Gold/Details | access-date = 6 February 2021}}</ref> 'Diabolo',<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Physocarpus opulifolius'' 'Diabolo'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/105625/Physocarpus-opulifolius-Diabolo-(PBR)/Details | access-date = 6 February 2021}}</ref> and 'Tuilad'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/249460/Physocarpus-opulifolius-Lady-in-Red-Tuilad-(PBR)/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder -''Physocarpus opulifolius'' Lady in Red = 'Tuilad' | accessdate = 25 April 2018}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 77 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 25 April 2018}}</ref>  Newer cultivars offer different foliage color as well as smaller overall plant size.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.extension.umn.edu/garden/yard-garden/trees-shrubs/common-ninebark/index.html|title=Common Ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius)|website=www.extension.umn.edu|language=en|access-date=2017-06-30|archive-date=2017-05-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170519204301/https://www.extension.umn.edu/garden/yard-garden/trees-shrubs/common-ninebark/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Ecology==
It is a larval host for the [[dimorphic eulithis]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bugguide.net/node/view/24345|title=Species Eulithis molliculata - Dimorphic Eulithis - Hodges#7203}}</ref> for ''[[Macaria abruptata]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bugguide.net/node/view/41771|title=Species Macaria abruptata - Hodges#6294}}</ref> the [[white spring moth]], ''Ancylis spiraeifoliana'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/data/hostplants/search/list.dsml?PSpeciesqtype=starts+with&PSpecies=opulifolius&PGenus=physocarpus&PFamilyqtype=starts+with&sort=Family&Familyqtype=starts+with&beginIndex=30&Speciesqtype=starts+with&Genusqtype=starts+with&PGenusqtype=starts+with&searchPageURL=index%2edsml%3fPSpeciesqtype%3dstarts%2bwith%26PSpecies%3dopulifolius%26PGenus%3dphysocarpus%26PFamilyqtype%3dstarts%2bwith%26sort%3dFamily%26Familyqtype%3dstarts%2bwith%26Speciesqtype%3dstarts%2bwith%26Genusqtype%3dstarts%2bwith%26PGenusqtype%3dstarts%2bwith|title = HOSTS - the Hostplants and Caterpillars Database at the Natural History Museum}}</ref> the [[Paonias excaecatus|blinded sphinx moth]], and possibly the [[Lomographa semiclarata|bluish spring moth]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/our-science/data/hostplants/search/list.dsml?searchPageURL=index.dsml&Familyqtype=starts+with&Family=&PFamilyqtype=starts+with&PFamily=&Genusqtype=starts+with&Genus=&PGenusqtype=starts+with&PGenus=physocarpus&Speciesqtype=starts+with&Species=&PSpeciesqtype=starts+with&PSpecies=opulifolius&Country=&sort=Family|title = HOSTS - the Hostplants and Caterpillars Database at the Natural History Museum}}</ref> The larvae of the [[raspberry leafroller]] have also been recorded on this plant.
